ai.literal: Return expecting-not duty; towards rain what will-do indeed world?
ai.translation: True duty expects no return. What can the world ever do in return for the rain?
ai.modern: கைம்மாறு எதிர்பார்க்காமல் உதவுவதே சிறந்த கடமையாகும். மழைக்கு இந்த உலகம் கைம்மாறாக என்ன செய்துவிட முடியும்?
ai.explanation: This couplet defines true benevolence as a duty that expects nothing in return. The word 'kaṭappāṭu' signifies a moral obligation to help others selflessly. The poet compares this unconditional giving to the rain, which sustains life without asking for anything back. By asking what the world could possibly give back to the rain, the couplet emphasizes that the highest form of giving is entirely one-sided.

ai.literal: Effort having exerted produced wealth all, to the worthy helpfulness doing for the sake of.
ai.translation: All the wealth produced by exerting great effort is for the sake of doing good to the worthy.
ai.modern: கடின முயற்சி செய்து ஈட்டிய செல்வம் அனைத்தும், தகுதியுடையவர்களுக்கு உதவி செய்வதற்காகவே ஆகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet explains the true purpose of earning wealth. The word 'தாள்' literally means foot or leg, but here it takes the accepted sense of effort or hard work. The wealth gathered through such industry is not meant for hoarding. Instead, its entire purpose is to perform acts of helpfulness or service ('வேளாண்மை') to those who are worthy or deserving ('தக்கார்க்கு').

ai.literal: Gods' even in the world and here obtaining is rare indeed than benevolence good other things.
ai.translation: Even in the world of the gods and in this world, it is rare indeed to obtain other good things better than benevolence.
ai.modern: தேவர் உலகத்திலும் இவ்வுலகத்திலும், ஒப்புரவை விடச் சிறந்த மற்ற நல்லவைகளைப் பெறுவது மிகவும் கடினமாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet emphasizes the supreme value of 'oppuravu', which means acting with benevolence and fulfilling one's duty to society. The poet states that finding anything better than this virtue is incredibly rare. He compares 'oppuravu' against all other good things ('nalla piṟa') and concludes it is unmatched. To stress its universal greatness, he notes that this holds true not just 'here' ('īṇṭum') in the human world, but even in the world of the gods ('puttēḷ ulakattum'). Thus, living in harmony with and helping society is presented as the highest possible good.

ai.literal: That which is fitting, the virtuous man, he lives a life; the other man, among the dead, to be placed he will be.
ai.translation: The virtuous man who does what is fitting truly lives. The one who does not will be counted among the dead.
ai.modern: உலக நடப்பிற்குப் பொருத்தமான அறத்தைச் செய்பவனே உண்மையில் உயிருடன் வாழ்பவன் ஆவான். அதைச் செய்யாத மற்றவன் இறந்தவர்களுக்குச் சமமாகவே கருதப்படுவான்.
ai.explanation: This couplet defines what it means to be truly alive in a society. The word 'ஒத்தது' refers to what is fitting or proper, pointing to one's duty to others. The virtuous man ('அறவோன்') who fulfills this social duty is the only one considered to be truly living ('உயிர்வாழ்வான்'). In contrast, the person who ignores this duty ('மற்றையான்') is completely useless to the world, and thus the poet says he will be counted among the dead ('செத்தாருள் வைக்கப்படும்').

ai.translation: The wealth of a man of great wisdom, whom the world loves, is like a village drinking pond filling with water.
ai.modern: உலகம் விரும்பும் பேரறிவாளனிடம் உள்ள செல்வமானது, ஊரின் நடுவே உள்ள குடிநீர்க் குளம் நீரால் நிறைந்தது போன்றதாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet compares the wealth of a wise and benevolent person to a village drinking pond full of water. A village pond is accessible to everyone and quenches the thirst of the whole community without discrimination. Similarly, when a person of great wisdom acquires wealth, they use it for the benefit of all, making them beloved by the world. The word 'பேரறிவாளன்' highlights that true wisdom naturally leads to such generous benevolence.

The wealth does not sit idle but becomes a cure for society's ills.

ai.translation: Those with the clear vision to know their duty will not shrink from benevolence, even in times when they have no wealth.
ai.modern: தங்கள் கடமையை அறியும் தெளிவான அறிவுடையவர்கள், தம்மிடம் செல்வம் இல்லாத வறுமைக் காலத்திலும் பிறருக்கு உதவி செய்வதிலிருந்து பின்வாங்க மாட்டார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the unwavering nature of true benevolence. The word 'இடன்' literally means space or place, but here it takes the sense of wealth or resources. Combined with 'இல் பருவத்தும்', it refers to a time of poverty or lack. Even in such difficult times, those who clearly understand their moral duty ('கடன் அறி காட்சியவர்') will not hesitate or shrink ('ஒல்கார்') from helping others. Their commitment to doing what is fitting for society does not depend on their financial comfort.

ai.translation: For a benevolent man, becoming poor is simply the state of being unable to bear not doing the fitting things he ought to do.
ai.modern: நற்பண்பு உடையவன் வறியவன் ஆதல் என்பது, தான் செய்யத் தகுந்த உதவிகளைச் செய்யாமல் இருக்க முடியாமல் வருந்தும் நிலையாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet defines what poverty truly means for a benevolent person. The word 'நயனுடையான்' refers to someone who possesses the goodness of helping others. For such a person, becoming poor ('நல்கூர்ந்தான் ஆதல்') is not about the personal lack of wealth. Rather, it is the painful state ('ஆறு') of being unable to rest ('அமைகலா') without doing ('செய்யாது') the fitting duties ('செயும் நீர') they are accustomed to performing for society.

ai.literal: By benevolence comes ruin if it is said, that a person having sold acquiring worth it possesses.
ai.translation: If ruin comes from doing one's duty to others, that ruin is worth a person selling himself to acquire.
ai.modern: பிறருக்கு உதவுவதால் ஒருவனுக்குக் கேடு வரும் என்றால், அக்கேடு ஒருவன் தன்னை விற்றாவது வாங்கிக்கொள்ளும் தகுதியை உடையது.
ai.explanation: The couplet explores the ultimate value of benevolence (ஒப்புரவு) by contrasting it with ruin (கேடு). It states that if helping others leads to one's own ruin or poverty, such a loss is actually a noble acquisition. The phrase 'விற்று கோள்' (selling to acquire) suggests that this kind of ruin is so honorable that a person should be willing to sell themselves or all they own just to obtain it. By using the language of commerce, the poet emphasizes that the moral worth of self-sacrifice far outweighs any material loss.
